interface.name: templar_shell_manager_v1

description.summary: shell control entry point

interface.description: Bound only by the client the compositor itself launched as the shell.

request.name: show_all_windows

description.summary: recovery view: every window, scattered across active outputs on the Recovery layer, with no reliance on the shell to compute the layout

request.description: Also compositor-keybinding-reachable with no shell running at all (`compositor/FORK.md`); this request exists so the shell can offer the same action from its own UI.

request.name: escape_fullscreen_or_modal

description.summary: compositor-level way out of a fullscreen or modal window

request.description: `toplevel` null escapes whichever window currently holds activation, if any. Also compositor-keybinding-reachable with no shell running (`docs/architecture/accessibility.md`).

request.name: set_layer_surface

description.summary: declare which typed layer a shell surface belongs to

request.description: Only `shell_overlay`, `notification`, `home_surface` and `system_modal` are valid here — `secure_lock` and `recovery` are compositor-owned and refused even for the shell; a client-side window's own layer (`normal` / `app_on_top`) is set through xdg-shell, not this request.

request.name: set_exclusive_zone

description.summary: reserve space along one edge of the output a shell surface is on

request.description:
A dock or panel asks for `size` logical pixels along `edge`, so that ordinary windows are placed beside it rather than beneath it. The compositor recomputes the affected output's work area (`templar_window::work_area_for`) and repairs any window this displaces.
This is a request, not an instruction. `templar_window::Output::usable` refuses a claim that would swallow the output, or that would leave too little room for a window's recovery band — the shell is a restartable, replaceable process and does not get the last word on whether the user can reach their windows. A refused claim is silently ignored rather than erroring: a shell that asked for too much should still run, just without its reservation.
`size` of 0 keeps the surface anchored to `edge` and reserves nothing; a surface destroyed releases its claim. A dock that shrinks to a hint is still a dock — the claim is what anchors it to its edge, so releasing it on 0 would leave the surface unplaced. Reservations are per surface, so a surface that is destroyed releases its own automatically, and that is the only thing that does.
The reservation is a floor on the surface's thickness, not its size: the surface is anchored to its edge and may commit a size thicker than it reserves — a bar opening a row above itself grows over the windows beside it without moving them, because the work area follows the zone and not the surface.
Along its edge the surface keeps its own committed extent, clamped to the output and anchored at the edge's start (the left end for `top`/`bottom`, the top end for `left`/`right`) unless it asks otherwise with `set_edge_alignment`. A strip narrower than the screen is a strip narrower than the screen: it reserves the same thickness whether it is showing two chips or a full row of them, so growing and shrinking it never reflows a single window. The compositor does not stretch a surface to fill its edge, and a surface is therefore never told how wide the output is by being configured to it — a shell that wants the full edge asks for it, from a size it already knows.
A shell surface holding a zone should stay mapped while a window is fullscreen rather than destroying itself to get out of the way. The compositor already handles it: a visible fullscreen client window sorts above `overlay` and `notification` on its own output (never above `system_modal`, and never above the lock or recovery surfaces the core owns), so the surface is simply covered. Destroying it instead releases the zone, which reflows every maximized window on that output twice — once on the way in and once on the way out.
That exception is suspended for as long as the pointer asks for it. When the pointer comes to *rest* on that output's bottom edge — outside the bottom-left corner square, which is the compositor's route to the Home Surface and is never this — the surface is drawn over the covering window again, and stays there while the pointer is either still on that edge or anywhere on the surface itself. No request is involved: the surface keeps painting exactly as it always does, its frame callbacks continue while it is covered, and nothing about its size, its zone or the work area changes on the way in or out. The compositor says so with `bar_peeked`, because the pointer is the compositor's to see — under a window filling the screen the surface never learns the pointer reached the edge at all, and a reveal it cannot see is a reveal it cannot answer.
A *maximized* window covers the bottom edge without outranking the overlay, so nothing about the stacking order changes for one; the edge is asked for and reported in exactly the same way, and the surface decides for itself what to do about it.

arg.name: size
arg.summary: logical pixels along that edge; 0 anchors and reserves nothing

request.name: reveal_home

description.summary: go home: hide every client window so the Home Surface shows, or bring them back

request.description: A view change only. No window is shelved, moved or deactivated by a reveal (`templar_window::WindowService::set_home_revealed`), so nothing is left to undo when it ends — and it ends on its own when a window is activated, a new window maps, a recovery action runs, or this connection goes away. Also compositor-keybinding-reachable (Ctrl+Alt+H on any keyboard; Super+D where there is a logo key; Escape while revealed). The compositor reports the resulting state through `home_revealed`, whichever side started it.

event.name: home_revealed

description.summary: whether a go-home reveal is currently in effect

event.description: Sent on bind and after every state change, keyboard-initiated ones included.

event.name: bar_peeked

description.summary: whether the pointer is asking for this output's bottom edge

event.description:
Sent on bind and after every state change. While set, a surface anchored to that output's bottom edge has been asked for by a pointer resting there, under a window that covers the screen (maximized or fullscreen); it is the surface's own business what to show, and collapsing to a hint until this arrives is the expected shape.
One output at a time, because there is one pointer. The empty string means no output is being asked for.

arg.name: output
arg.summary: the output's name, or empty for none

request.name: arrange_windows

description.summary: arrange every eligible open window per a named preset

request.description: User-invoked arrangement, never a standing tiling policy (`templar_window::WindowService::arrange_windows`). The first request retains each eligible window's geometry and maximize state as the one baseline; switching presets recomputes from that baseline and the current eligible set — never from the previous preset's result — so presets can be auditioned by pressing buttons. Windows that closed are ignored; windows that opened join on the next explicit request; fullscreen and shelved windows are never touched. The compositor remains the sole geometry authority: the shell only names the preset and renders the buttons.

request.name: restore_arrangement

description.summary: return every surviving window exactly to the retained baseline

request.description: Geometry and maximize state come back exactly as they were before the first preset, repaired only where the output topology no longer reaches the old rectangle (`templar_window::repair_window`); the baseline is then spent. A request with no retained baseline does nothing.

description.summary: the named arrangements, mirroring templar_window::ArrangementPreset

request.name: set_idle_timeout

description.summary: how long the session may be idle before the screen turns off

request.description:
The compositor is the session's only honest idle source — it sees every input event, and nothing else in the session does. The *policy* is not its to decide: `org.templaros.Power1` records `screen_off_after` per power source, the shell reads it, and this request is how the number reaches the one process that can act on it. Sent on connect and again whenever the stored value changes.
`seconds` of 0 means never. Any other value arms a countdown that restarts on every keyboard, pointer and touch event, and that is suspended entirely while any `zwp_idle_inhibit_manager_v1` inhibitor is alive. On expiry the compositor turns every output off (DPMS off on real hardware); the next input turns them back on.
Turning the screen off is *not* locking it and not dimming it. `Power1`'s `lock_after` and `dim_after` are separate intervals with separate meanings, and neither is enforced by this request.

arg.name: seconds
arg.summary: idle seconds before the screen turns off; 0 never

request.name: set_terminal

description.summary: which application is the drop-down terminal

request.description:
The terminal chord (`Super+grave`) is a compositor keybinding, so it keeps working with the shell dead; but *which* terminal is a Providers1 choice (the `terminal` role), made in Settings and read by the shell. This request is how the choice reaches the compositor: the canonical application id of the selected terminal, sent on connect and again whenever the selection changes. An empty string means no terminal is selected.
With a terminal named, the chord toggles that application's most recently activated window: shelved or absent from the top, it is unshelved and activated; on top and focused, it is shelved (never closed — a stray press must cost nothing) and focus returns to the window that had it. With no such window mapped, the compositor sends `terminal_requested` and the shell launches the provider through the ordinary launch chain, so identity still comes from the cgroup.

arg.name: app_id
arg.summary: canonical application id, or empty for none

request.name: set_edge_alignment

description.summary: where along its edge an anchored shell surface sits

request.description:
`set_exclusive_zone` decides which edge a surface is anchored to and how much of the output it reserves; it says nothing about where along that edge the surface sits, and the compositor's own answer is the edge's start. This request is how a shell says otherwise: `start`, `centre` or `end` of `edge`.
This is placement, never reservation. The alignment moves the surface along its edge and changes nothing about the work area — a centred strip reserves exactly what the same strip reserves at the start, and a zone of 0 still reserves nothing wherever it sits. Moving a surface from one alignment to another therefore reflows no window, for the same reason that growing it along its edge does not.
The alignment applies only to a live `set_exclusive_zone` claim on the same `edge`. A surface that never sends this request, or that sends it for an edge it does not claim, is anchored at the start — which is what every surface did before this request existed. Like a zone, an alignment is per surface and is released when the surface is destroyed.

request.name: open_taskfield

description.summary: open the window overview, filtered

request.description:
Taskfield is the compositor's window overview: the scene pulls back and the live windows become the interface. It is a **view, not a place** — HomeGarden is the desktop, and this is a temporary projection of the windows that already exist. It is laid out when it opens and thrown away when it closes; no card position is ever stored against a window, and there is deliberately no request to save one.
The chord (`taskfield.open`), the Peek corner and `window.show-all` open it from the compositor with `all`. This request is the shell's routes into it: a chip with more windows than its fan can hold (`unit`, `key` naming the application or `group:ID`), a launcher result's arrow (`unit`), a HomeGarden place's "N windows active" line (`windows`, `key` carrying the place's name for the header), and the shelf band (`shelved`). The compositor never learns what a place is — the shell sends the ids.
`key` is empty for `all` and `shelved`; `windows` is empty unless `filter` is `windows`. Ignored while the session is locked or the recovery overlay is up, and ignored when the filter selects nothing: an overview of no windows is indistinguishable from a black screen, so there is nothing to enter.

arg.name: key
arg.summary: application id, group:ID, or a place's name; empty for all and shelved

arg.name: windows
arg.summary: window ids as uint32, for the windows filter only

event.name: terminal_requested

description.summary: the terminal chord was pressed and no terminal window exists

event.description: The shell answers by launching the `terminal` provider. Sent at most once per press.

event.name: group_cycle_binding

description.summary: the chord that opens the window overview, for the cheat sheet

event.description:
Sent on connect: 0 is `Super+Tab` (the default). Reserved so a future setting can move the chord without a protocol change; the shell renders whatever it is told.
Since version 8 that chord opens Taskfield rather than cycling between window groups — the overview shows every group as a section, which is the same question asked properly. The name is the shipped one and does not change; only what the chord does did.

event.name: taskfield_state

description.summary: the window overview opened, changed or closed

event.description:
Sent on entry, on every query or selection change, and on leave (`active` 0). The mode's state lives in `templar_window` and the compositor owns its keys, so this event is the shell's whole view of it: it maps its `presentation` layer surface while `active`, draws the header for `filter`/`key`, echoes `query` into its search field and rings `selected`.
The shell does not receive the cards' rectangles. It computes them by running the same `templar_window::taskfield::layout` over the toplevels it already holds and the outputs it already knows — the same function on the same bytes, so the labels cannot land anywhere but on the cards. A shell that is not running changes none of this: the compositor draws its own labels and the mode works exactly as well.

arg.name: active
arg.summary: 1 while the overview is up, 0 when it closes

arg.name: selected
arg.summary: the selected window id, or 0 for none

event.name: launcher_focus

description.summary: reveal Home with the Apps bar focused and armed

event.description: `Super+Space` does not open a second launcher: the Apps bar on Home is the one launcher object (`@templaros.decision.the-home-field-is-a-launcher-not-a-search`), and this is one more route into it. The compositor has already revealed Home when it sends this; the shell moves the caret into the Apps bar. Under a fullscreen window the reveal hides client windows without unfullscreening any of them, so the route out of fullscreen to starting something is `Super+Space`, type, Enter — and the fullscreen window is undisturbed.

description.summary: which windows the overview shows

entry.name: unit
entry.summary: one application or window group, named by key

entry.name: windows
entry.summary: an explicit list, in the windows array

entry.name: start

description.summary: the left end of a top/bottom edge, the top end of a left/right one

entry.description: The default, and what every surface got before `set_edge_alignment` existed.

entry.name: presentation

description.summary: the window overview's chrome

entry.description: Titles, section headers, the query field and `+n more`, drawn over the windows the compositor is presenting. Mapped only while the overview is up and unmapped the moment it closes; it is configured to the whole output and reserves nothing. Above `shell_overlay`, and above the half step a fullscreen window takes over it, because the overview is explicit navigation and a fullscreen window may not cover it.

entry.name: home_surface

description.summary: the bottom layer: the Home Field itself

entry.description: Visible by default, because it is the desktop. The compositor hides it only while a visible fullscreen or maximized client window covers the same output, and shows it regardless while a `reveal_home` reveal is in effect. The shell does not decide this and need not track it: it draws its Home surface once and leaves it mapped.

request.name: join_group

description.summary: put this window in `other`'s group

request.description: If `other` is in no group, a new group is made of the two. If both are in groups, the groups merge and `other`'s identity (id, name, accent) survives. The compositor also places this window beside `other` — the nearest free side — when it is not already adjacent, exactly as a band dropped on `other`'s band does.

request.name: activate_group

description.summary: raise every member together, this window on top, and focus it

request.description: A trusted-shell activation like `activate`, but the token is checked once for the group; the Home tile's title press uses it.
